newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: CAUTION URGED ON ASIAN INVESTMENT SURVEY
The Prime Minister has urged caution when reading the results of a survey of Asian business attitudes towards Australia in the wake of the race debate.

Opposition leader Kim Beazley has told Parliament the survey, conducted by the Far-Eastern Economic Review, shows the majority of business leaders in many Asian countries are less likely to invest in Australia.
John Howard says anti-Asian rhetoric will never be part of the attitude of the Coalition government and he's again welcomed the contribution of Australians of Asian descent.
GOVERNMENT UNDER FIRE OVER AD FUNDING
The Federal Government's been accused of using taxpayers' money to fund a blatantly political advertising campaign centreing on its new family tax initiative.
Labor's Senate Leader, John Faulkner, is asking how much the television ads are costing, and whether proper tender processes were followed in awarding the advertising contract.
The Government claims up to two million Australian families will benefit from a series of tax concessions promised by the Coalition during the election campaign.
PLANS TO IMPROVE HUMAN RIGHTS
Australia is to push for the establishment of an International Criminal Court.
Foreign Minister Alexander Downer says his government has identified three proposals it will pursue to improve human rights and democracy.
Mr Downer says Australia will also give funds to strengthen human rights institutions in the Asia Pacific region, and support the establishment of a Centre for Democratic Institutions in Australia.
But he says setting up an International Criminal Court will be a major priority in the next two years.
HOWARD TO REFLECT ON 1996
The Prime Minister will tomorrow reflect on his government's achievements as its first year in office draws to a close.

At the final party room meeting for the year today, John Howard delivered a pre-Christmas pep talk to his colleagues. He said his government's been more stable and successful in its first year than the Fraser Government was, and it can look forward to long years in power if party members are sensible and resolute.

He'll make an end of year statement to the nation in parliament tomorrow about the events of the year and the future. Mr Howard's indicated there won't be any announcement on the Republic or the Head of State until the New Year.
NEW HIGH FLYER ENTERS THE MARKET
A new cut-price airline enters the tough trans-Tasman market this week.
Central Pacific Airlines will operate between Auckland and Brisbane three times a week, and between Auckland and Melbourne once a week.
The new airline will use a Boeing 737 jet -- leased from Air Nauru.
The trans-Tasman market has already claimed one financial casualty this year -- budget priced Kiwi International Airlines collapsed in September.
But Central Pacific says it's confident it can succeed.
Chief executive Jeff Mathews says other airlines have increased their trans-Tasman fares since Kiwi went out of business -- and there's strong passenger demand for a budget-priced service.
COLSTON SAYS DISSOLUTION THREAT INFLUENCED TELSTRA VOTE
Queensland Independant Senator Mal Colston has acknowledged the threat of a double dissolution election was a factor in his decision to strike an agreement with the Government on Telstra.
Senator Colston is one of the two independants who's support will allow the sale to pass Parliament.
Senator Colston has joined Tasmanian Independant, Brian Harradine in acknowledging the threat of a snap election played a part in his decision.

He says he's confident the Government would have called a double dissolution if the Senate had twice rejected the Telstra sale ... and says there would have been no chance of winning concessions if a joint sitting of Parliament had voted on the bill.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
